pages.api:
# API

> What the cog publishes and what it answers.

## Stream: `iq.cs16/<source>` (`iq.cs16.v1`)

One ring record is a 40-byte header and then complex samples (little-endian i16 I, Q; 12 significant bits). The header carries the segment (one per dwell), the centre, rate and bandwidth, the sample index on the segment's clock, the samples lost just before it, and flags (discontinuity, band changed, all zero). A gap is also written as its own record with no samples. IQ stays on the node; it is not exported by default.

## Reading: `sdr.status/<source>` (`sdr.status.v1`)

`telemetry.v1`-style items: LO, rate, bandwidth, gain, RSSI, temperatures, delivered, expected, lost, pending, gap events, overflows, zero blocks, retunes.

## Service: `svc.sdr/<source>`

`tune`, `set_rate`, `set_bw`, `set_gain`, `plan`, `plan_remove`, `lease`, `release`, `status`, and `tx_config`, which is always refused. Tuning refers to the caller's own plan; several callers' plans take turns. A lease is exclusive for up to an hour.

## HTTP (loopback)

`/status`, `/raw?samples=N`, `/guide`, `/healthz`.

## Store vector (id 29)

`[centre GHz, rate MS/s, power dBFS, loss fraction, PHY temp C, Zynq temp C, zero-block fraction, gap events]`.
pages.connect:
# Connect the radio

> Right port, right power, an antenna on the receive port, and room to cool.

## Plug orientation

The Pluto has two USB-C ports.

- One goes to a CH340 USB-serial bridge. It is the Linux console and nothing else. If this is the only port plugged into the computer, the radio does not appear, although a port (`1a86:7523`) does.
- The other is the Zynq's own USB port, which carries libiio. It enumerates as `0456:b673` and brings the network gadget (`192.168.2.1`, RNDIS) on Linux.

Plug the computer into the Zynq port. Check with `lsusb | grep -i 0456` (Linux) or `system_profiler SPUSBDataType` (macOS). A port appearing is not proof: the bridge has its own power, so it enumerates with the radio dead.

## Power

The Pluto draws from its USB port. A laptop or board port that browns out ends the session. Put a charger or a powered hub on the other (console) port if you see disconnects; the Ventuno Q runs it that way and the board's power monitor shows no draw from its own port.

## Antenna

Use the receive port, RX port A (the cog selects it). The stock whip antennas work indoors for FM, ADS-B at 1090 MHz and 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Do not connect a transmitter, an amplifier output or a dummy load to the receive port without an attenuator: the input is not protected against more than about -10 dBm.

## Heat

The Zynq idles near 60 degrees C in open air and the AD9364 near 40. Both are in `hw.temp_zynq_c` and `hw.temp_phy_c`. Next to a busy board, give the Pluto airflow. A rising Zynq temperature with no change in load is the first sign to look at.

## Receive only

On start the cog switches digital loopback off, switches the DDS tones off and sets the transmit attenuation to its maximum (-89.75 dB), and records what it found in `safe_state`. A crashed earlier client can leave loopback on, which makes the receive path read zeros; the cog also treats an all-zero stream as a fault.
pages.range:
# Frequency range and rates

> 70 to 6000 MHz measured, 325 to 3800 MHz rated; what each limit means.

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Declared range | 70 to 6000 MHz (the measured range, after the firmware's AD9364 setting) |
| Rated range | 325 to 3800 MHz (the AD9363's specification) |
| Sample rate | 0.521 to 61.44 MS/s on the chip; 5 MS/s continuous on the Ventuno Q |
| Bandwidth | 0.2 to 56 MHz |
| Gain | -3 to 71 dB manual, or the chip's slow-attack AGC |

Outside the rated range the cog still tunes, and marks every band it reports there `uncalibrated`: the noise floor is about 5 dB worse and there are spurs above 4 GHz. Use readings there for presence and shape, not for levels.

Below 2.083 MS/s the chip needs its decimating FIR; the cog loads one when you ask for a lower rate and switches it off again when you ask for a higher one.

A rate above 7.5 MS/s over USB 2.0 loses samples. The cog still runs it and reports the loss.
pages.setup:
# Set up

> Install the cog, run it once, then let the node start it.

Needs libiio 0.19 to 0.26 (`apt install libiio0`; on macOS `brew install libiio`). The cog loads the library when it opens the radio, so a host without it still runs `--simulate`. On Linux a udev rule must give your user access to the radio (`0456:b673`) if you use `usb:`; the network gadget (`ip:192.168.2.1`) needs none.

```
cog-sdr-pluto-rx --once                         # one 3 s capture window, then the report
cog-sdr-pluto-rx --once --simulate              # no radio
cog-sdr-pluto-rx --band-plan 2437e6:5e6:2000,1090e6:2.4e6:1000,915e6:2e6:1000
cog-sdr-pluto-rx --once --record cap.iq         # keep the window as a capture file
cog-sdr-pluto-rx --once --replay cap.iq         # play it back
```

A band is `centre_hz:rate:dwell_ms[:bandwidth[:gain]]`. One band streams continuously; several take turns, one dwell each, and the report shows how long each plan ran.

The backend is chosen when the cog starts: it measures `ip:192.168.2.1` and `usb:` for about a second each and uses the faster (on the Ventuno Q, `ip:`). `--backend ip|usb|auto` and `--uri URI` override.

The stream goes to the node's cogbus when `WEFTOS_COGBUS` and `WEFTOS_COGBUS_TOKEN` are set. `GET /status`, `/raw`, `/guide` and `/healthz` are on `127.0.0.1:8063` (`--api-bind`).
pages.start:
# Start here

> One cog owns the PlutoSDR, streams its samples to the node, and says how many it lost.

`sdr-pluto-rx` opens the radio through libiio, puts it in a known receive-only state, and publishes what it hears as the `iq.cs16.v1` stream on the node's cogbus. Other cogs (spectrum, ADS-B, decoders) read that stream; none of them open the radio.

## The short path

1. **Plug the radio in the right way round.** The Pluto has two USB-C ports and only one of them is the radio. → see **Connect**
2. **Check the antenna and the heat.** → see **Connect**
3. **Run the cog.** `cog-sdr-pluto-rx --once` prints one report; without hardware it says `no_source`. → see **Set up**
4. **Read `samples`.** `delivered` against `expected`, and `lost`, tell you whether the link kept up. → see **Troubleshoot**

You can try everything with no radio: `--simulate` makes a synthetic signal marked `SYNTHETIC`, and `--replay FILE` plays back a capture made with `--record FILE`.

## How the signal flows

```diagram
flow
```

## Honest limits

- The data path is USB 2.0. About 7.5 MS/s is the ceiling, 5 MS/s is gap-free on the Ventuno Q; above that samples are lost, and the cog counts them.
- The 70 to 6000 MHz range is measured, not rated. The chip is rated 325 to 3800 MHz; outside that band levels are not calibrated.
- The stream carries no hardware timestamps. Loss is counted from the host clock; see **Troubleshoot** for what that can and cannot resolve.
- Receive only. The cog never enables a transmit buffer and refuses `tx_config`.
pages.troubleshoot:
# Troubleshoot

> Read the counters before suspecting the radio.

| Symptom | Likely cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `no_source`, `libiio not found` | Install libiio, or set `LIBIIO_PATH` to the library. |
| `no_source`, no radio on the backend | Wrong USB port (see **Connect**), no power, or the radio is rebooting; the cog waits and reopens. |
| `dead_receive_path` | Every sample is zero. Digital loopback was left on, or the front end is not running. The cog switches loopback off when it takes the radio; if it persists, replug the radio. |
| `samples.lost` rising | The link cannot keep up. Lower the rate (5 MS/s is safe over USB 2.0), use `ip:` on Linux, or close other users of the USB bus. |
| `pending_unconfirmed` large, `lost` small | A loss is in progress and not yet confirmed (about 0.25 s). |
| `disconnects` rising | The radio dropped off the bus: power or cable. The cog logs it and reopens; it never power-cycles anything. |
| `apply_errors` | A band outside the tuning range or a rate the chip refused; `error` says which. |

## What the loss count can and cannot tell you

The stream has no hardware timestamps and an overflow is silent. The cog counts samples against the host clock. A loss is declared when the shortfall stays above 20 ms of data for 0.25 s, so:

- a loss shorter than about 20 ms is indistinguishable from USB jitter;
- a loss rate under about 0.1 percent is indistinguishable from the crystal's drift;
- a gap is reported about 0.25 s after it happened, and the sample clock jumps then.

`samples.expected` and `samples.delivered` are the raw comparison and are always honest; `lost` is the part the cog is sure of.

toml:
# Sensor guide for sdr-pluto-rx (WeftOS ADR-104 sensor-guide format, schema 1).
# Pages are Markdown files next to this one (guide/<page>.md). The radio is a USB device, so
# there is no header pinout or wiring: the only diagram is the signal flow.

schema = 1
title = "PlutoSDR receive on a Linux board"
sensor = "PlutoSDR Nano (Zynq-7010 + AD9363A, run as AD9364) over USB, libiio"
cog = "sdr-pluto-rx"
cog_version = "0.1.0"
medical = false
pages = ["start", "connect", "range", "setup", "troubleshoot", "api"]

# Checklist step ids the companion app links to a page.
[links]
sensor_found = "connect"
plug_orientation = "connect"
power = "connect"
antenna = "connect"
heat = "troubleshoot"
range = "range"
cog_installed = "setup"
cog_running = "setup"
export = "setup"
no_source = "troubleshoot"
loss = "troubleshoot"

# Signal flow, left to right.
[[flow]]
name = "Antenna"
detail = "RX port A, 70-6000 MHz measured"

[[flow]]
name = "AD9363A / AD9364"
detail = "LO, filter, ADC, up to 56 MHz"

[[flow]]
name = "USB 2.0"
detail = "7.5 MS/s ceiling, 5 MS/s safe"

[[flow]]
name = "libiio"
detail = "ip: on Linux, usb: on macOS"

[[flow]]
name = "sdr-pluto-rx cog"
detail = "owner, band plans, loss counted"

[[flow]]
name = "Outputs"
detail = "iq.cs16.v1 ring, sdr.status, svc.sdr"
